terms.gloss: I’m better; with tibi, sibi, the person who is better
evidence: Cic. Fam. 16.22: Spērō ex tuīs litterīs tibi melius esse
Cic. Att. 6.7.2: sed nūntiant melius esse, of Tiro
Cic. Fam. 16.5: cum meliuscule tibi esset
terms.comment: Cicero’s way of saying that a sick person is better: the impersonal melius est with the dative, meliuscule for “a little better”.

terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation; ex morbō, from an illness
evidence: Dolabella in Cic. Fam. 9.9.1: certum sciō jam convaluisse eam
terms.comment: Getting better, as against feeling better: jam convaluisse eam, that she is better now (Dolabella, of Terentia).

phrases.english: He’s getting better; maybe he’ll be up tomorrow.

phrases.latin: Spērō ex tuīs litterīs tibi melius esse, cupiō certē.
phrases.english: From your letter I hope you are better; I certainly want you to be.
But they report that he is better (of Tiro, left behind seriously ill).

phrases.latin: tē plānē febrī carēre et bellē habēre
phrases.english: that you are quite free of fever and doing nicely

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 56, 98, 314.
